content: 1. E.L., Ferng Y.H., Wong-McLoughlin J., et al. conducted a study examining the effects of non-pharmaceutical interventions on the incidence of upper respiratory infections (URIs) and influenza in densely populated urban households. 2. Agah R., Cherry J.D., Garakian A.J., et al. investigated the rate of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections among healthcare personnel caring for children with RSV. They compared routine isolation procedures with those supplemented by the use of masks and goggles. 3. Somogyi R., Vesely A.E., Azami T., et al. explored the dispersion of respiratory droplets when using open versus closed oxygen delivery masks, highlighting implications for the transmission of severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS). 4. Foo C.C., Goon A.T., Leow Y.H., et al. conducted a descriptive study in Singapore on adverse skin reactions caused by personal protective equipment (PPE) used during the SARS outbreak. 5. Gala C.L., Hall C.B., Schnabel K.C., et al. 6. Loeb M., Dafoe N., Mahony J., et al. performed a randomized trial comparing the effectiveness of surgical masks versus N95 respirators in preventing influenza among healthcare workers. 7. Pelke S., Ching D., Easa D., et al. assessed whether the use of gowns impacts colonization or infection rates in neonatal intensive care units, finding no significant effect. 8. Broderick M.P., Hansen C.J., Russell K.L. examined the effectiveness of social distancing in reducing respiratory pathogen transmission, considering environmental contributions. 9. Doherty J.A., Brookfield D.S., Gray J., et al. studied the practice of cohorting infants with RSV to reduce nosocomial transmission. 10. Isaacs D., Dickson H., O'Callaghan C., et al. investigated the role of handwashing and cohorting in preventing hospital-acquired RSV infections. 11. Yen M.Y., Lin Y.E., Su I.J., et al. described the use of an integrated infection control strategy to minimize nosocomial SARS infections among healthcare workers during outbreak control. 12. Simon A., Khurana K., Wilkesmann A., et al. 13. Macartney K.K., Gorelick M.H., Manning M.L., et al. 14. Krasinski K., LaCouture R., Holzman R.S., et al. demonstrated that screening for RSV and assigning patients to cohorts upon admission can reduce nosocomial transmission. 15. Wang T.H., Wei K.C., Hsiung C.A., et al. 16. The CDC reported on the efficiency of quarantine during the 2003 SARS epidemic in Beijing, China. 17. Ou J.M., Dun Z., Li Q., et al. evaluated the effectiveness of the quarantine system during the SARS epidemic in Beijing in 2003. 18. Cowling B.J., Lau L.L., Wu P., et al. studied the role of entry screening in delaying local transmission of the 2009 H1N1 pandemic influenza. 19. Heymann A., Chodick G., Reichman B., et al. 20. Heymann A.D., Hoch I., Valinsky L., et al. 21. Potter J., Stott D.J., Roberts M.A., et al. demonstrated that influenza vaccination of healthcare workers in long-term care hospitals reduces mortality among elderly patients. 22. Lemaitre M., Meret T., Rothan-Tondeur M., et al. conducted a cluster-randomized trial showing that influenza vaccination of nursing home staff reduces resident mortality. 23. Hayward A.C., Harling R., Wetten S., et al. evaluated the effectiveness of an influenza vaccination program for care home staff in preventing death, morbidity, and healthcare use among residents. 24. Saito R., Suzuki H., Oshitani H., et al. studied the effectiveness of influenza vaccination against H3N2 virus infections in nursing homes in Niigata, Japan, during the 1998–1999 and 1999–2000 seasons. 25. Oshitani H., Saito R., Seki N., et al. examined the relationship between influenza vaccination levels and influenza-like illness in long-term care facilities for the elderly during an H3N2 epidemic in Niigata, Japan. 26. Ando R., Kaname S., Yoshida M., et al. surveyed novel H1N1 influenza infection and vaccination in dialysis facilities in the Tokyo Tama area. 27. Kanaoka S. investigated the influence of inpatient and personnel vaccination on influenza outbreaks in long-term medical and care hospitals. 28. Thomas R.E., Jefferson T., Lasserson T.J. reviewed the impact of influenza vaccination for healthcare workers who care for the elderly. 29. Stevenson C.G., McArthur M.A., Naus M., et al. assessed the prevention of influenza and pneumococcal pneumonia in Canadian long-term care facilities. 30. Shugarman L.R., Hales C., Setodji C.M., et al. analyzed the influence of staff and resident immunization rates on influenza-like illness outbreaks in nursing homes. 31. Carman W.F., Elder A.G., Wallace L.A., et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial showing that influenza vaccination of healthcare workers reduces mortality among elderly residents in long-term care. 32. Weinstock D.M., Eagan J., Malak S.A., et al. described the control of influenza A in a bone marrow transplant unit. 33. Engels O., Goldman N., Doyen M., et al. reported that immunization of healthcare workers reduced the nosocomial burden of influenza A in a pediatric hospital. 34. Monto A.S., Rotthoff J., Teich E., et al. studied the detection and control of influenza outbreaks in well-vaccinated nursing home populations.
